opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I should say up front that ageing biology isn't my core area, so take this as an informed outsider's view rather than an expert one.

The basic problem is simple: ageing is slow, and the outcome you care about is slower still. If you want to know whether an intervention extends healthy human lifespan, the direct experiment means enrolling people and waiting decades to see who gets sick and who dies. That's a brutal constraint on iteration speed. In most fields where we've made fast progress, like machine learning, you can run an experiment, see what happened, and adjust within days or weeks. In human ageing research, your feedback loop is roughly a human lifetime, and you only get a few loops per career.

People work around this in a few ways, each with real limits. One is model organisms: worms, flies, mice. You can run many lifespans quickly, and we've learned a lot that way, but translation to humans is unreliable. Lots of things that extend mouse lifespan don't obviously do anything for people, and the reasons are only partly understood.

The second is biomarkers and surrogate endpoints: epigenetic clocks, frailty measures, and so on. If you trusted a biomarker, you could run a trial over a couple of years instead of thirty. The catch is that you have to validate the biomarker against the outcome you actually care about, which brings back the slow feedback loop. And there's a Goodhart's law risk: an intervention might move the clock without moving the underlying biology.

The third is targeting specific diseases of ageing rather than ageing itself. That fits the existing regulatory framework better, because there are clinical endpoints you can measure. But it may push you toward treating symptoms one at a time rather than the shared upstream causes.

So I think the time constraint is one of the main bottlenecks, possibly the main one, and the most valuable work is whatever shortens the feedback loop credibly. That could be better-validated surrogate markers, better models of human biology, or more computational and mechanistic understanding, so you're not relying entirely on waiting and watching. There's an interesting question about whether more capable AI changes this. It might speed up the hypothesis-generation side a lot, but it doesn't obviously remove the need to eventually check things in real humans over long periods. Physical-world experimentation stays a bottleneck even if the thinking gets much faster.

r001.rationale: The response says biomarkers and surrogate endpoints could let researchers assess an intervention in a couple of years instead of waiting decades, while noting they need validation.

r002.rationale: It says work in worms, flies, and mice has taught researchers a lot, but does not say that this has contributed to treatments improving human wellness; it emphasizes that translation to humans is unreliable.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the central bottlenecks, and it's underappreciated how much of it is just a clock you can't speed up. If you want to know whether an intervention extends human lifespan, the honest experiment takes decades, because the outcome you care about is at the end of a long process. You can run that experiment in mice in two or three years, in flies in a couple of months, in yeast in days, and that's exactly why most of what we know comes from those organisms. But every time you move down that ladder you're trading time for relevance, and the translation from a short-lived animal to a human is where a lot of promising results quietly die.

So the field has largely been forced into surrogate endpoints. Instead of waiting to see whether people live longer, you measure something you believe tracks ageing: epigenetic clocks, inflammatory markers, frailty indices, the rate at which some biomarker drifts. The whole game then becomes whether those surrogates are actually causally connected to the thing you want, or whether you're just moving a dial that happens to correlate with age. That's a hard scientific question in its own right, and I don't think it's solved. The FDA doesn't recognise ageing as an indication partly for this reason; you can't run a trial for something you can't measure on a reasonable timescale.

The other way around it is to borrow time that's already elapsed. There are people who've been taking metformin or rapamycin or living under caloric restriction for long periods, and observational data on them is informative, though badly confounded. Biobanks with decades of longitudinal samples let you look backwards rather than forwards. And there's a lot of hope that better models of biology, including machine learning on those datasets, can compress the inference so you need less wall-clock time per bit of evidence.

My honest view is that the time constraint means progress will be lumpy rather than smooth. You'll see interventions that look good on surrogates and get adopted on faith, and then thirty years later you find out which ones were real. That's uncomfortable, but it's also how a lot of medicine has actually worked. The thing I'd push on is making the surrogates much better, because that's the lever that shortens the loop, and almost everything else downstream depends on it.

r001.rationale: It describes measuring ageing-related surrogate endpoints instead of waiting to learn whether people live longer, presenting this as a way to shorten the evidence-gathering loop.

r002.rationale: It says research in smaller organisms supplies much of what is known, but does not state that this research has contributed to treatments that improve human wellness.

astra-6.text:
I think it puts a pretty fundamental limit on how fast you can know that something works. Even if you could come up with a promising treatment very quickly, you still have to wait to see what happens to the people who receive it. And if the thing you care about is whether they live longer and stay healthy, that can take a long time.

You can try to get around that by studying shorter-lived animals, or by measuring biomarkers that you think indicate biological age. But then you have this extra question: does changing that measurement actually mean you’ve slowed ageing in humans? You might make the indicator look better without improving the outcome you care about.

So I’d distinguish the speed of generating treatments from the speed of establishing that they’re safe and effective. AI could potentially help a lot with the first, and help us design better experiments for the second. But it doesn’t automatically remove the need to observe what happens over time.

r001.rationale: It says to observe treated people’s health outcomes to learn whether a treatment works, but does not identify this as a way to learn without waiting a human generation.

r002.rationale: It mentions studying shorter-lived animals as a possible approach, but does not state that research on smaller organisms has already contributed to treatments that improve human wellness.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a pretty fundamental constraint. Even if AI makes the process of coming up with candidate treatments much faster, it doesn’t automatically make the experiments faster. If you want to know whether something extends a human life, the most direct experiment takes a very long time.

You can get evidence sooner from short-lived animals, or from measuring things that you think are indicators of ageing. But then the question is how well those results predict what you actually care about. A treatment might improve a biomarker without making people live longer or stay healthy for longer.

So I’d distinguish between making the intellectual work faster and making the feedback loop faster. AI could help enormously with the first, and perhaps help us find better ways to do the second. But I wouldn’t assume that solving the biology intellectually means we can immediately establish that a treatment works safely in humans.

r001.rationale: The response mentions short-lived animals and ageing indicators as earlier evidence, but does not identify measuring a person’s health after an intervention as a way to learn its effects without waiting a human generation.
